summary: For upper KS2 (ages 9–11), move children from naming healthy behaviours to reasoning about how everyday choices affect specific body systems, and crucially that effects are usually cumulative and delayed — it is the pattern over months and years, not a single biscuit or late night, that shapes health. Teach through MECHANISM on systems already studied (circulatory, respiratory, digestive), frame outcomes as changes in RISK not certainty, and handle sensitive content (weight, substances) factually and without stigma. Core activity: a 'lifestyle over time' simulation where repeated choices compound, complemented by an evidence-weighing conversation with an expert, a tap-to-reveal body reference, a personal-pulse measurement, and consolidation items matching choice to internal effect.
misconceptions: 'One unhealthy thing will make you ill / one healthy thing keeps you well' — missing that it's the cumulative pattern that matters.
'You can see straight away if something is unhealthy' — missing the delayed onset of many effects.
'Being thin = healthy and being larger = unhealthy' — conflating body size with health; focus on systems and behaviours, factually and without stigma.
'Some foods are poison / totally banned' — rather than amount-and-frequency within an overall balance.
'Exercise is only about losing weight' — missing that it strengthens the heart, lungs and muscles regardless of weight.
'Smoking/alcohol only harm you when you're old' — missing that damage accumulates from the start.
'Health outcomes are certain' — rather than changes in RISK/probability.

activities.title: Lifestyle over time: watch choices compound
steps: Steer a character week by week, setting choices each simulated week: meals, how much exercise, how much sleep, and whether to smoke or drink.
Watch heart, lung, weight and energy gauges respond slowly — notice that no single choice moves the needle much.

Run the clock forward across many weeks and observe patterns compounding: a mostly-active, balanced character's heart and lung gauges strengthen, while a sedentary, high-sugar, smoking character's gauges drift the other way and the disease-risk meter rises — toward a higher CHANCE, not a certainty.
Replay two lifestyles side by side to compare how accumulation over time, not any one day, built the difference.
Tap any gauge to read how that choice acts on the actual body system (e.g. 'smoking damages the alveoli so less oxygen reaches the blood').
activities.insight: Health is built or eroded by the accumulation of everyday choices over time; single choices barely register, but repeated patterns change how body systems function and shift the RISK of disease.

activities.title: Ask the doctor: weigh a health claim
steps: Ask a friendly doctor or body-systems scientist your real questions in role, e.g. 'what does smoking actually do to my lungs?'
Weigh the answer, which is grounded in mechanism and risk, and respond when gently probed ('why do you think that?').
Bring an evidence question to settle, e.g. 'what's my evidence that exercise makes the heart stronger, not just the arm and leg muscles?'
activities.insight: Health messages are evidence-based claims to reason about, not rules to obey; you can obtain information from an expert and combine it with what you know to judge a claim.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal body: choice to organ
steps: Tap an organ on a body diagram to reveal how diet, exercise, smoking and alcohol affect it.

Build a choice-to-system-to-effect chain for each organ, e.g. exercise to heart and breathing muscles to stronger; smoking to lungs to less oxygen and higher heart-disease risk; sugary diet to teeth (higher risk of decay) and a diet high in saturated fat to heart and blood vessels (higher heart-disease risk); alcohol to liver and brain.
Use it as a reference layer to check mechanism links encountered in the simulation.
activities.insight: Each lifestyle choice acts on a specific body system, so health advice can be understood mechanistically rather than memorised as isolated rules.

activities.title: Connect it to your own pulse
steps: Measure your resting heart rate, then your heart rate just after exercise, drawing on the earlier heart-rate topic.

Use the immediate difference as evidence that the heart works harder during exercise; and, over a period of regular activity, compare your resting pulse before and after that period to look for adaptation, taking several readings at the same time of day and when calm, and remembering that resting pulse also changes with things like illness, tiredness or excitement, so a small change may not show adaptation.
Explain what this shows about exercise working the heart itself, not just the arm and leg muscles.
activities.insight: Exercise works the heart itself: a pulse that rises during and after exercise shows the heart working harder, and a resting pulse that stays lower (measured carefully under similar conditions) after a sustained period of regular activity fits with the heart adapting and strengthening over time — not just a slogan, and not only about limb muscles.

activities.title: Consolidate: match, judge, interpret
steps: Match each choice to the body-system effect it causes.
Judge a given health claim as reasonable or not and say why, using mechanism and risk.
Interpret a simple data/timeline item showing how an effect builds up cumulatively over time.

Reason about transfer cases: how two people of the same weight can differ in heart health; why a frequently sugary diet raises the risk of tooth decay even without weight gain; whether a fit marathon runner's exercise cancels out their smoking.
activities.insight: You can distinguish health from mere appearance by naming a specific internal harm, and you can read cumulative effects from data over time.

checkQuestion: Someone says: 'I'm slim and I feel fine, so it doesn't matter that I eat lots of sugary, fatty food, never exercise, and I've started smoking.' Choose one part of the body that is being harmed anyway, even though they look fine — and explain what is actually happening inside that they can't see.
checkAnswer: These choices damage the body internally even without a visible weight change: sugary food causes tooth decay and, with fatty food, raises the risk of heart disease; lack of exercise leaves the heart, lungs and muscles weaker; smoking damages the lungs and increases heart-disease risk. Looking slim or feeling fine doesn't mean the heart, arteries, lungs or teeth aren't being harmed.
